existing_incident_edges.relationship: Race and the Education of Desire (1995) questioned the marginal place of race and empire in Foucault's history of sexuality while using his 1976 lectures; Carnal Knowledge asked 'why Foucault's elusive and suggestive treatment of race still remains so marginal to what colonial historians take from him today' (2002, p. 141, as quoted by Ottevaere)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md P.9 2) re-sourced this arrow from post to the new person entry ann_laura_stoler, keeping its id and kind, because its claim was hers alone. Earlier note retained: the checked publisher description of Race and the Education of Desire (1995) records a critique of the marginal place of empire, and of race in the making of bourgeois sexuality, in Foucault alongside productive use of his 1976 lectures and Dutch and French colonial archives; the book itself is unread; Spivak's critique of Foucault is the separate edge from her person entry. Added: Ottevaere 2004 (read in full), quoting Carnal Knowledge, p. 141 ('why Foucault's elusive and suggestive treatment of race still remains so marginal'), and ch. 6, 'A Colonial Reading of Foucault' (UC Press contents); Schultz 2015 (read): 'First it was Michel Foucault's Collège de France lectures about the biopolitics of race'.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Sexuality and racial formation investigated through colonial archives: 'the micromanagement of sexual arrangements … was critical to the distinctions between ruler and ruled' (1995, as quoted by Gouda); 'sexual control was both an instrumental image for the body politic … and itself fundamental to how racial policies were secured' (2002, p. 78, as quoted by Ottevaere)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md P.9 2) re-sourced this arrow from post to the new person entry ann_laura_stoler, keeping its id and kind. Earlier note retained: the 1995 project both uses and questions Foucault; this contribution is the specific colonial-historical intervention described by the publisher, not the origin of queer history or proof that all queer historians adopted it. Added: Gouda 2009, p. 553 (read in full), quoting the 1995 book without a page; Ottevaere 2004 (read in full), quoting Carnal Knowledge, p. 78.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Asked colonial studies to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' and from 'extractive' to 'ethnographic' archival work (2002); read the Dutch colonial archive 'along the grain' for 'the pulse of the archive' and set out 'to set a new standard for an ethnography of the archives' (2009, pp. 35, 45, as quoted by Schulte Nordholt)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own words: the 2002 abstract (read); the 2009 book's pp. 32–33, 35 and 45 as quoted by Schulte Nordholt (read in full), and pp. 3, 5, 24, 41, 43, 53 as quoted by Gouda (read in full). Both books unread. data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md §§1–2.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: With Cooper, an agenda for reading metropole and colony together (1989; 1997); Carnal Knowledge argued that 'students of colonialism, anthropologists in particular, have taken the politically constructed dichotomy colonizer/colonized as a given rather than as a historically shifting pair of social categories' (2002, p. 13, as quoted by Ottevaere, 2004); Gouda: homage to her work 'has become de rigueur' in postcolonial studies
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Ottevaere 2004 (read in full), quoting pp. 9, 13 and 15; Gouda 2009, pp. 553–554 (read); Crossref for the 1989 introduction; the graph's existing record of Tensions of Empire (contents). The 1989 and 1997 introductions are unread. The post entry's strands colonial_intimacies and metropole_colony already name her.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: 'Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power: Gender and Morality in the Making of Race' (ch. 3, 2002): 'Ethnographies of empire should attend both to changing sensibilities and to sex, to racialized regimes that were realized on a macro and micro scale' (p. 78, as quoted by Ottevaere, 2004); métissage as 'the tension between a form of authority simultaneously predicated on incorporating and distancing' (p. 83, as quoted by Ottevaere); 'Like Joan Scott', she evaluates 'historically designated categories' (Ottevaere)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Ottevaere 2004 (read in full), quoting pp. 78 and 83 and making the Scott comparison; UC Press contents (read). Chapter unread.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: 'An ethnography of the archives' as a standard for the discipline (2009, p. 45, as quoted by Schulte Nordholt), against 'doing an ethnography in the archives'; her 2002 complaint that anthropologists' 'archival activity tends to remain more an extractive than an ethnographic one'; Schulte Nordholt: good historians 'are less often accustomed to making archives into an object of ethnographic research'
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Stoler 2002 abstract (read); Schulte Nordholt 2009, pp. 560–562 (read in full).

existing_incident_edges.relationship: 'Memory-Work in Java: A Cautionary Tale' (2002, ch. 7) 'situates memories of domestic service by those who served against the density of the archives around them' (p. 162) and 'invites more work on colonial memory itself while making the "colonial" a subject rather than an assumed category of analysis' (p. 203, as quoted by Ottevaere)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Ottevaere 2004 (read in full), quoting pp. 162 and 203; UC Press contents (read). Chapter unread.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: 'Tense and Tender Ties: The Politics of Comparison in North American History and (Post) Colonial Studies' (JAH 2001; Haunted by Empire, 2006) brought postcolonial critiques to North American history and questioned the conventions of comparison (Duke description); Imperial Debris (2013) asked colonial scholars 'to move beyond the theoretical and empirical limitations of postcolonial and subaltern studies' toward ongoing 'ruination' (Schultz)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Duke page for Haunted by Empire (contents and description, read); Crossref for the 2001 article; Schultz 2015 (read in full), quoting 'violent verb' (p. 7) and 'what people are left with' (p. 9); Duke page for Duress (contents: 'On Degrees of Imperial Sovereignty'). Bodies unread; the comparison claim rests on a publisher description.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Perry named Stoler (with McClintock, Said and Burton) in the 'international literature on gender and colonialism' that inspired On the Edge of Empire (2001), with a caution about analysing 'white discourse and white discourse alone' (1995); Perry later wrote 'The Colonial Archive on Trial' in Burton's Archive Stories (2005)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Rests on the evidence already recorded for edge_1023 (post → adele_perry): Perry's own 2001 statement and her 1995 caution, read in an earlier revision (pe139_perry_presence_2001, pe139_perry_sick_1995); Burton's contents (Duke page, read). The person-level arrow makes the influence that edge_1023 attributes to a field attributable to its named author; edge_1023 itself is unchanged. Perry's chapter is unread.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Burton draws on Stoler’s emphasis on colonial regimes’ precarious vulnerability when explaining why imperial culture should not be treated as an irresistible juggernaut.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Burton explicitly pairs Stoler’s formulation with John Darwin’s chaotic pluralism as interpretive postures making room for agency and resistance while retaining empire’s coercive power. Darwin’s co-credit is preserved; he has no current endpoint. This is a bounded conceptual use, not general agreement with every Stoler argument, personal mentoring, or a body-reading claim for Along the Archival Grain.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Stoler uses Trouillot’s account of archival power to examine how histories are authorized and silenced.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own Stoler 2002, 93/n24 pairs Trouillot with David W. Cohen, and 96/n38 explicitly cites Trouillot 55 on previous understandings/archival power. 98/n49 adds a particular reference. Stoler’s Netherlands Indies research and other analytical sources remain her own distinct intervention; not claim Trouillot founded the whole archival turn.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Bush identifies Stoler’s work on archives and historical production as a theoretical resource informing Fuentes’s reading of enslaved women’s fragmentary records.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Actual Bush 2017 publisher extract 46 explicit informed by theoretical developments and names Burton, Stoler, Trouillot WITH others, citing Fuentes 5. Collective attributed resource, not exclusive influence or claim exact original works/editions read. Whole Bush review and Fuentes book unread. Schmitt 8 generic Stoler field framing is NOT sole evidence for arrow; this is distinct explicit mediation.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Carter uses Stoler’s account of colonial bourgeois formation to explain the policing of European marital dissent as well as colonized domestic life.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2008:31/note 44 and 64/note 1 explicitly quote Stoler and apply the argument to interracial unions and other alternatives to monogamy. The cited authored chapter is Cultivating Bourgeois Bodies and Racial Selves in Catherine Hall’s edited Cultures of Empire (2000), 87–88 and 90. Hall’s editorial role is distinct; the original Stoler chapter is unread here. This bounded resource does not certify all Carter’s historical generalizations or convert her whole career into a single paradigm.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Cooper credits collaboration with Stoler for developing a research agenda on colonial societies through the interplay of historical inquiry and anthropology.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2017 reprint:343–344/notes 15–17 explains that similarly framed studies of East African and Sumatran agriculture led to shared conferences, the 1989 American Ethnologist papers and the jointly edited Tensions of Empire (1997). He describes theory and empirical work as mutually informative. Stoler is a collaborator with her own research, not Cooper’s formal teacher, sole origin of colonial studies, or author of every contribution. The 1989 and 1997 introduction bodies and Stoler’s monograph remain unread here; existing source metadata and group route are preserved.

named_group_routes.relationship: Foucault supplies a named resource that sexuality historians adapt and question
named_group_routes.evidence_note: D’Emilio’s 1983 note 1 explicitly acknowledges Foucault, McIntosh and Weeks while arguing that a wage-labor explanation remains necessary. Stoler’s 1995 project critically extends Foucault into colonial history. This supports specific reception, not a sole origin of the field.

named_group_routes.relationship: Mohanty and Stoler make gendered colonial relations part of postcolonial inquiry
named_group_routes.evidence_note: A gender-history contribution; distinct textual and archival projects.

named_group_routes.relationship: Foucault criticised for discounting individual authors (1978) and for ignoring empire and dissolving the individual in a 'microphysics of power' that it is 'hopeless to resist' (1993)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (1978): 'Foucault believes that in general the individual text or author counts for very little; empirically, in the case of Orientalism (and perhaps nowhere else) I find this not to be so' (p. 23), while declaring himself 'greatly indebted' to Foucault (p. 23). Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993): of Foucault and Raymond Williams, 'In the main I am in considerable sympathy with the genealogical discoveries of these two formidable scholars, and greatly indebted to them. Yet for both the imperial experience is quite irrelevant, a theoretical oversight that is the norm in Western cultural and scientific disciplines' (p. 41). Comparing Foucault and Fanon: 'Foucault's work moves further and further away from serious consideration of social wholes, focussing instead upon the individual as dissolved in an ineluctably advancing "microphysics of power" that it is hopeless to resist'; 'ignoring the imperial context of his own theories, Foucault seems actually to represent an irresistible colonizing movement that paradoxically fortifies the prestige of both the lonely individual scholar and the system that contains him'; Foucault 'swerves away from politics entirely' (p. 278). His note 198 refers the reader to 'my critique in "Foucault and the Imagination of Power"' (in David Hoy, ed., Foucault: A Critical Reader, 1986, pp. 149–155); that essay, and 'Traveling Theory' (1983), were not read. On p. 26 he also describes Foucault's turn to 'the local micro-physics of power that surround the individual'. Foucault's position is given only as Said presents it; no reply by Foucault was looked for. The critique is from a writer who kept using Foucault (edge 2); it is a disagreement within an acknowledged debt. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) records other postcolonial critics' engagements and stays.

named_group_routes.relationship: Foucault's account of power criticised as blind to imperialism and the international division of labour, and for an intellectual who lets the oppressed 'speak for themselves' while remaining transparent; his analyses of disciplinary institutions kept as useful (1988)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period text: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint, read in full). She takes as her object ‘Intellectuals and power: a conversation between Michel Foucault and Gilles Deleuze’ (p. 66), whose participants ‘systematically ignore the question of ideology and their own implication in intellectual and economic history’ (p. 66). In her summary of the conversation, ‘the oppressed can know and speak for themselves’ (p. 74); she adds ‘to Said’s analysis the notion of the surreptitious subject of power and desire marked by the transparency of the intellectual’ (p. 75). ‘Foucault is a brilliant thinker of power-in-spacing, but the awareness of the topographical reinscription of imperialism does not inform his presuppositions’ (p. 85); ‘The clinic, the asylum, the prison, the university - all seem to be screen-allegories that foreclose a reading of the broader narratives of imperialism’ (p. 86). She keeps part of his work: ‘what remains useful in Foucault is the mechanics of disciplinarization and institutionalization, the constitution, as it were, of the colonizer’ (p. 90), and calls his model of localized resistance ‘an admirable program’ that, universalized, ‘accommodates unacknowledged privileging of the subject’ (p. 85). Foucault’s position is given only as she presents it, from the translated conversation and Power/Knowledge; no reply was looked for (he died in 1984). Reception: Eagleton (1999, read) groups Derrida and Foucault as thinkers who ‘veer between a cult of theoretical “madness” ... and a more restrained, reformist sort of politics’, a criticism of her allies, not a defence of Foucault. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) carries her name with Stoler’s; see the optional relabel. Said’s separate critique of Foucault is pe137_said_rel_04 (said draft); she cites Said’s criticism and extends it (p. 75).

named_group_routes.relationship: Feminist and postcolonial work on gender, race and colonial categories (Stoler and McClintock, as she and her reviewers name them, with Said and Burton) as the 'international literature on gender and colonialism' that she said inspired On the Edge of Empire (2001), used with a caution about analysing 'white discourse and white discourse alone' (1995)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words. 2001 (BC Studies 132, p. 58, read): the book 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism'; 'Edward Said's Orientalism contains the germinal insight that such stock knowledge functioned to inform and serve the centre rather than to understand the various peripheries about which, putatively, it spoke' (pp. 58–59); Burton's argument, as Perry puts it, that knowledge of margins should 'unpack the intimate wedding of historical scholarship to the nation-state' (p. 59, citing Burton in Catherine Hall's Cultures of Empire reader); Anne McClintock's 'anachronistic space' (p. 61); Chakrabarty 'convincingly argues' that history cannot be disaggregated 'from the politics of Western supremacy that produced it' (pp. 63–64). 1995 (p. 43, read), on scholars of colonial discourse who 'analyse white discourse and white discourse alone': the position 'contains an important critique of the intellectual conceit' in historians' attempts to represent the colonized, but 'it can also function to legitimize the neglect of First Nations histories'. In-period reviewers, their characterisations: Rutherdale (Labour/Le Travail 50, 2002, p. 325, read): 'Influenced by the work of Anne Laura Stoler, Perry argues that because "white and Aboriginal people shared ties, homes, children, and labour," they "challenged colonialism's foundational fiction"' (p. 123 of the book), and the book is 'informed by an international post-colonial, feminist, gendered, and Marxist analysis'; Orlowski (Left History 8:1, 2002, pp. 119–120, read): she is 'positioned within feminist postcolonial scholars such as Ann Laura Stoler, Robert J. C. Young, and Anne McClintock, all of whom she refers to in the book', and she uses 'discourse' in 'the Foucauldian sense', though she 'never defines' it (p. 121). The book itself is unread, so the influence of Stoler rests on the reviewers' statements. Stoler, McClintock and Burton have no atlas entries; Stoler is on the post roster (colonial_intimacies) and the gender roster (colonial_categories), Said has a person entry.

named_group_routes.relationship: Stoler's 2002 essay addresses anthropologists engaged in postcolonial studies; Dirks, Burton and Arondekar likewise examine colonial archives
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Stoler 2002 abstract (read): its first sentence names post-colonial studies; From the Margins and Archive Stories contents (Duke pages read); Arondekar's Duke page (read). No body read; narrowed after review (finding 8) to the texts' stated subjects, with no founding or first-object claim. data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md P.1.4.
named_group_routes.map_label: Colonial archives in Stoler, Dirks, Burton and Arondekar, 2002–09

named_group_routes.relationship: Archive Fever (1994/1996), a text explicitly engaged by Cook, Steedman and Burton: Cook dated a 'Derrida aftershock' in which historians and anthropologists subjected 'the archival world to a detailed critique such as it has never before experienced' (2001); Steedman's AHR essay (2001) and Burton's introduction (2005) carry his title
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Cook 2001, p. 21 (read); Steedman's and Burton's titles (Crossref; Duke contents); Stoler 2002, n. 21, and Schwartz and Cook 2002, nn. 15 and 17, cite Archive Fever (reference lists read). The existing arrow edge_588 (derrida → memory) is not repeated; this one carries the archive readership.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Archaeology's 'The Statement and the Archive' and 'Nietzsche, Genealogy, History' are the Foucault the turn cites: Stoler's 2002 notes open with the latter and twice cite the former; Cook names 'Foucault's historical methodology' among his own exposures (2001); Manoff's survey begins from Derrida and Foucault (2004)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Stoler 2002 reference list (nn. 1, 30, 42; read); Cook 2001, n. 23 (read); Manoff's abstract (DSpace record). Thin: rests on citations, not on a passage stating the debt.

named_group_routes.relationship: An editorial comparison: Cook presented the archival profession's engagement as 'postmodernism and the practice of archives' (2001) and Manoff found 'a confluence of interests among scholars, archivists, and librarians' begun by Derrida and Foucault (2004), while Stoler's programme reads 'along the grain' before reading against it (as Gouda puts it, 2009)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Cook 2001 title and abstract (read); Manoff's abstract (DSpace record); Gouda 2009, p. 552 (read). An editorial comparison placed by the atlas, not a succession claimed by any text read; no text read names the linguistic turn as its target (reworded after review, finding 8).

named_group_routes.relationship: Silencing the Past (1995) placed the archive inside the production of history: silences enter at 'the moment of fact creation (the making of sources)', 'fact assembly (the making of archives)', 'fact retrieval (the making of narratives)' and 'retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)'; 'in history, power begins at the source' and 'archives are the institutions that organise facts and sources' (all as quoted by Davidson, 2020); Stoler's 2002 essay cites it three times
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Davidson 2020 (read, unpaginated), which reproduces the four-moments passage as a block quotation ('Silences enter the process of historical production at four crucial moments: the moment of fact creation (the making of sources); the moment of fact assembly (the making of archives); the moment of fact retrieval (the making of narratives); and the moment of retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)') and quotes 'in history, power begins at the source' and 'archives are the institutions that organise facts and sources' as Trouillot's words; Beacon contents; Stoler 2002 nn. 24, 38, 49 (reference list read). Body unread; corrected after review (finding 13). Wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1 (precedent: the Chandavarkar 1997 quotations in 1.152).
named_group_routes.map_label: Silences and the making of archives, 1995
